title: VPC route flap and DNS fallback diary
content:
Short goal: capture breadcrumbs for the private-deployments egress + DNS flakiness incident. Mostly a personal notebook — commands, quick outputs, hypotheses, and next steps. Save this for postmortem skeleton and to avoid repeating the same re-runs later.

Summary of symptom:
- Intermittent failures from on-prem customer VM to Redwood-hosted control-plane endpoints (TLS timeouts, TLS handshake failures ~20% of requests). Failures more frequent during peak egress.
- Symptoms appear as: API client errors (timeout, "handshake failure"), occasional certificate mismatch (SNI showing different CN in logs), and DNS failures where system resolver falls back to internal DNS then times out.
- Affected env: private deployment in customer VPC peered to Redwood via shared VPC peering (multi-AZ).

Quick timeline (local notes):
- 2025-11-12 09:10 initial report from SE: "customer sees 503s to control-plane for 10-15m"
- 2025-11-12 09:18 I asked for tcpdumps and traceroutes (collected)
- 2025-11-12 09:25 noticed traceroute path changes mid-failure window — possible route flap
- 2025-11-12 10:05 reproduced locally in staging when simulating heavy egress (burst of 500 connections/sec)
- 2025-11-13 added ip route / route-table audit; found overlapping route in peered account
- 2026-01-07 tested TLS handshake with s_client: intermittent SNI->CN mismatch (weird)

Commands I ran (raw):
- ip route show table 100
  -> 10.40.0.0/16 via 10.128.0.1 dev eth0 proto static metric 100
- ip route get 10.128.2.65
  -> returns via 10.128.1.1 dev eth1  (flip-flops sometimes)
- sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host 10.128.2.65 -w /tmp/dump1.pcap (captured flapping TTL/DF bits)
- sudo tcptraceroute -n 10.128.2.65 443
  -> shows intermittent second-hop blackhole (RST vs no reply)
- sudo iptables-save | grep -i conntrack
  -> nothing obvious, conntrack table not saturated (conntrack -L shows entries)

TLS / openssl experiments:
- openssl s_client -connect 10.128.2.65:443 -servername control.redwood.internal -tls1_2 -msg
  -> sometimes completes: "Verify return code: 0 (ok)"
  -> sometimes hangs at "SSL_connect:errno=104" (connection reset)
- openssl s_client -connect control.redwood.internal:443 -servername control.redwood.internal
  -> resolves via DNS to 10.128.2.65; same intermittent failures
- curl -v --resolve control.redwood.internal:443:10.128.2.65 https://control.redwood.internal/health
  -> success (on good windows) or "Failed to connect" (during failure windows)

Observed logs/snippets (sanitized):
- kernel: RTNETLINK answers: File exists (seen on route add in peered VPC sync)
- gostack: at 2025-11-12T09:27:41Z connection to 10.128.2.65 timed out (1000ms)
- envoy (control-plane): "client_cert: CN=control-az1, SNI=control.redwood.internal -> client IP 10.128.2.101"
- during failures: SNI value in access logs sometimes blank for same source IP (indicates TCP-level reset or TLS renegotiation failing)

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Asymmetric routing: request enters via one peering/route table but return traffic leaves via different NAT or peering path, causing stateful middleboxes to drop TLS handshake continuation. Evidence: traceroute flipped mid-window, ip route get returns different next-hops.
2) Overlapping/duplicate route propagation: a stale route in peered account briefly takes precedence, causing traffic to blackhole to a dark pool. Evidence: RTNETLINK "File exists" during route sync; found a /16 overlap between dev and prod peering.
3) DNS fallback path: internal resolver tries primary internal DNS; when DNS server in one AZ is overloaded it times out forcing fallback to secondary which points to different endpoint IP (older control-plane) -> SNI mismatch. Evidence: clients show DNS TTLs short and occasional NXDOMAINs during peak.
4) SNAT variance across AZs: NAT gateway IP differs between AZs; some of our control-plane routing uses SNI-based routing that expects specific source IP ranges and otherwise refuses (rare config), causing handshake issues. Evidence: source IP observed in logs varies by AZ and failed sessions cluster by source IP.
5) Conntrack exhaustion: briefly considered but counters fine. Put lower probability.

What I tried to validate/falsify each hypothesis:
- Asymmetric routing:
  - setup continuous ping+tcpdump on both sides during load test. Captured packets where SYN arrives at control-plane, SYN-ACK leaves different interface (sequence numbers show reply route mismatch).
  - ran ip monitor route on both peered VPCs while flipping an aggressive route advertisement script; saw route table changes coincide with packet loss windows.
  -> conclusion: asymmetric routing is plausible and likely necessary condition.

- Overlapping route propagation:
  - audited Terraform states across accounts; found an overlapping 10.128.0.0/16 in a stale dev env that was supposed to be 10.129.0.0/16.
  - asked infra-owner to rollback the stale route advertisement; after soft rollback we observed a reduction in event frequency (not elimination).
  -> conclusion: overlapping route contributed but didn't fully explain intermittent DNS timeouts.

- DNS fallback/dnsmasq oddities:
  - captured systemd-resolve queries: primary internal DNS (10.10.0.2) got overloaded and served truncated responses occasionally; client then retried to 169.254 resolver which returned old A record (10.128.1.22).
  - tested: echo -e "nameserver 10.10.0.2\nnameserver 10.10.0.3" > /etc/resolv.conf then stressed primary: saw same effect.
  -> conclusion: resolver behavior (retry/fallback) amplifies issue. Need to increase DNS capacity or adjust client retry/backoff.

- SNAT variance:
  - compared source IP in access logs for successful vs failed sessions; failed sessions correlated with a small set of NAT allocation ranges in AZ-b.
  - asked network team to check SNI-routing rules that might whitelist source ranges — found a legacy acl that treated requests from older NAT pool differently (bug).
  -> conclusion: SNAT+ACL bug was real and increased failure probability when return path used that AZ's NAT. Fixed via config change (pending deploy).

Temporary mitigations we applied during incident windows:
- disabled the stale dev route advertisement (rollback in Terraform) — immediate improvement but not full resolution.
- temporarily pinning control-plane egress to single AZ to avoid cross-AZ SNAT variance (reverted after confidence increased).
- increased DNS query worker pool on internal resolver (bump from 50 -> 200). Reduced DNS truncation events.

Metrics to collect for postmortem (what I will add to the ticket):
- per-AZ distribution of successful/failed TLS handshakes (by source IP and NAT range)
- route table change events and timestamps correlated with failed sessions
- DNS query latency percentiles during windows
- conntrack max usage and overflow events
- tcpdump samples (pcap) correlated to failure windows (save 3+ representative captures)

Next steps (actionable):
- (SEV follow-up) Schedule a brief runbook update to include route overlap checks and DNS capacity checks before peering changes.
- (Infra) Ensure route advertisement PRs include automated overlap checks with existing peering blocks (CI check).
- (Net) Deploy fix to ACL that mishandled requests from legacy NAT pool; monitor TLS failure rate for 48h.
- (Platform) Consider making TLS routing not depend on source IP for internal control-plane endpoints — or ensure NAT pools are stable.
- (Ops) Add DNS client retry jitter and reduce hard failover to fallback resolver in our internal client library.

Notes for postmortem narrative (brain-dump):
- Root cause is multi-factor: overlapping route + DNS fallback + legacy NAT/ACL. Individually none of them would always cause users to see failures, but combined with high load they create an intermittent failure mode.
- Operational fixes: remove overlapping route sources; harden DNS resolver capacity; eliminate SNI-routing by source IP or stabilize NAT pools.

Random commands and captures to keep:
- sudo tcpdump -i any -w /tmp/peering-flap-20251112.pcap 'host 10.128.2.65 or host 10.128.1.22'
- sudo ss -ntp | grep 10.128.2.65
- ip monitor route > /tmp/route-changes.log &
- journalctl -u systemd-resolved --since "2025-11-12 09:00" --until "2025-11-12 10:30" > /tmp/dns-logs.txt

Questions still open / TODOs for investigation:
- Confirm whether any BGP-like route propagation is involved (cloud-level peering propagation logs?). We have hints of propagation delay but need cloud provider telemetry.
- Get list of all NAT allocation ranges per AZ for the customer's VPC and compare to ACLs on control-plane LB.
- Long-term: can we make control-plane endpoints tolerant to source IP churn for internal customers?

If I forget: key takeaway = asymmetric/overlapping routing + DNS fallback jitter + legacy ACL = intermittent TLS failures. Fixes already in progress: route rollback, DNS capacity bump, ACL change MR in review (gitlab MR 312).

End of scratchpad. Will tidy into a PM-friendly postmortem skeleton once we confirm BGP propagation logs and MR deploys.
